# Introduction

Let $X$ be a random variable, $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be an i.i.d. sample from
$X.$ Let $X_{(1)},\ldots,X_{(n)}$ be the order statistics associated
with $X_1,\ldots,X_n.$ As we learnt in school the (empirical) mean
($\bar{\mu}_0$) and median ($\bar{\mu}_1$) of $X$ are defined
respectively by $$\bar{\mu}_0=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i,$$
$$\bar{\mu}_1   = \begin{cases}
        X_{(m+1)}  & \text{if}\  n=2m+1, \\
      \frac{X_{(m)}+X_{(m+1)}}{2} & \text{if}\ n=2m.
      \end{cases}$$ Both quantities $\bar{\mu}_0$ and $\bar{\mu}_1$ are
used in practice as estimates of the "center\" of the distribution of
$X.$ Let $F$ be the cumulative distribution function of $X,$ the
theoretical mean of $X$ defined by $$\mu_0=\int x \mathrm{d}F(x)$$ does
not always exist. To the contrary the theoretical median of $X$ given by
$$\mu_1=\inf\{ x:\ \  F(x)\ge \frac{1}{2}\}$$ always exists. Besides
this existence issue, medians are very important in practice because
they are resistant to outliers. This means that they are not heavily
affected by a very high or a very low value of the data. Median
computation is used in many fields. For seismic data processing we can
cite [@Ste:85]. In image processing, median filters are preferred to
mean filters because of their edge enhancement properties. Applications
involving median computation can be found in [@HuYaTa:79], [@NoGa:82],
[@AzPeTo:23] and [@YINeALL:96]. As mention in the literature (see for
instance [@Tib:09]), median is more appropriate than mean to measure the
center of a population. However the appealing qualities of the median
come with a high price: computing the median takes more time than
computing the mean. For this reason, many methods for computing median
have been devised. The methods based on the "divide and conquer\"
principal are developed in [@Hoa:61], [@Tib:09] and [@AzPeTo:23]. These
methods are very interesting and significantly faster than the "sort
then select\" method implemented in most computer languages. However
they do not always give us what we expect to get. Indeed, when $n=2m$,
they return $X_{(m)}$ or $X_{(m+1)}$ and none of these quantities is the
median given in textbooks. In [@Sat:22] is introduced a novel iterative
method to approximate the median. Although this method appears to be
interesting, it is not shown in the paper, how to choose the parameter
used in its construction. Another class of iterative methods that can be
used to compute the median of a data set is the subgradient. The
sugradient method is a conventional means to minimize a nonsmooth
function, therefore it can be used to compute the median by minimizing
the sum of absolute deviations. Good expositions of the subgradient
algorithm can be found in [@Tib:17] and [@Ma:19]. The class of
subgradient methods shares some characteristics of the methods introduce
in this paper:

- They build sequences "converging\" to the median.

- The sequences are build using the left hand side (one-sided)
  derivative of the sum of absolute deviations.

The approaches of this paper and the class of subgradient methods also
have some ingredients or properties that are very different. For
example:

- The subgradient class builds a sequence $(x_n,n\in {\mathbb N})$ such
  that $$\lim x_n=\bar{\mu}_1$$ where $\bar{\mu}_1$ is the sample
  median. While the class of methods developed in this article builds
  two (adjacent) sequences
  $(a_n,n\in {\mathbb N}), \quad (b_n,n\in {\mathbb N})$ such that
  $$a_n\leq \bar{\mu}_1 \leq b_n \quad \text{and}\quad \lim( b_n-a_n)=0.$$

- The output of our approaches is the *exact* median $\bar{\mu}_1,$
  whereas the output of the subgradient class an *approximate* value of
  $\bar{\mu}_1.$

The aim of this article is to introduce methods which return the median
as they teach it in school and at the same time, on average, outperforms
the conventional "sorting\" method for "large" sample size.

The next section contains theoretical foundations of the methods
introduced in this paper. The common principles of our algorithms are
presented in Section 3. The dichotomic method is outlined in Section 4
and the last section of the paper contains the gradient descent method.

# Theoretical preliminaries  {#sec:2}

Let $x\in{\mathbb R}$, the sum of absolute deviation of the sample
$X_1,\ldots,X_n$ from $x$ is given by
$$\varphi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lvert X_i-x\rvert.$$ It is well-known that
the median of $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is a minimizer of the function $\varphi$,
in others words $$\varphi( \bar{\mu}_1) =\inf_{x} \varphi(x).$$ Lemma 1
below is fundamental, it gives us useful information about $\varphi.$
The proof of Lemma 1 is in the supplementary material. In order to state
this result we introduce the following notations. Let
$Y_1<Y_2<\ldots<Y_m$ be such that
$$\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\}=\{Y_1,\ldots,Y_m\}.$$ Set $$\begin{align*}
          S = &\{Y_1,\ldots,Y_m\}, \\
          I_0= & (-\infty,Y_1), \quad I_1=[Y_1,Y_2),\ldots, I_{m-1}=[Y_{m-1},Y_{m}),\quad I_m=[Y_m,+\infty).
\end{align*}$$

::: lemma
**Lemma 1**. * *

- *For $k\in \{0,\ldots,m\},$ $\exists \alpha_k, \beta_k\in{\mathbb R}$
  such that
  $$\varphi(x)=\alpha_k x+ \beta_k, \quad \forall x\in I_k.\quad \quad\quad\quad$$*

- *For $j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, $\exists q_j\in{\mathbb N}^*$ such that
  $$\alpha_j- \alpha_{j-1}=2 q_j.$$*

- *$\quad \quad-n=\alpha_0 <\alpha_1<\ldots <\alpha_{m-1}<\alpha_m=n.$*
:::

We are now going to introduce the definitions and notations, we will use
to state the next theorem. The right hand derivative of $\varphi$ at
$a\in {\mathbb R}$ is defined by
$$\varphi'_+(a)=\lim_{\substack{h\to 0 \\ h>0}} \frac{\varphi(a+h)-\varphi(a)}{h}.$$
Similarly the left hand derivative is given by
$$\varphi'_-(a)=\lim_{\substack{h\to 0 \\ h<0}} \frac{\varphi(a+h)-\varphi(a)}{h}.$$
Let $a_0\in{\mathbb R},$ $a_0$ is called

- a **mininum** of $\varphi$ if
  $$\forall x\in{\mathbb R},\  \varphi(a_0)\leq \varphi(x),$$

- an **absolute mininum (am)** of $\varphi$ if
  $$\forall x\in{\mathbb R}\setminus\{a_0\},\  \varphi(a_0)< \varphi(x).$$

In the sequel we dote by $\mathscr{M}$ the set of minimum of $\varphi$
ı.e.
$$\mathscr{M}=\{a\in{\mathbb R},\ a \ \text{minimun of} \ \varphi\}.$$
We make use of the following definitions below.

- A point $a_1$ of ${\mathbb R}$ is called the **least mininum (lm)** of
  $\varphi$ if $$a_1=\min\left(\mathscr{M}\right).$$

- A point $a_2$ of ${\mathbb R}$ is called the **greatest mininum (gm)**
  of $\varphi$ if $$a_2=\max\left(\mathscr{M}\right).$$

We have the following foundation result whose proof is in the
supplementary material.

::: theorem
**Theorem 1**. *For any data set $S=\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\},$ one and only
one of the following two statements ((a), (b)) is true.*

- *$\varphi$ has an **absolute mininum (am)** $a_0$ satisfying:*

  - *$a_0\in S,$*

  - *$a_0$ is the only point satisfying
    $$\varphi'_-(a_0)<0 \quad\text{and}\quad \varphi'_+(a_0)>0.$$*

- *$\varphi$ has a **lm** $a_1$ and a **gm** $a_2.$ Furthermore in this
  case we have:*

  - *$a_1,\ a_2\in S,$*

  - *$\mathscr{M}=[a_1,\ a_2]$*

  - *$a_1$ is the only point satisfying
    $$\varphi'_-(a_1)<0 \quad\text{and}\quad \varphi'_+(a_1)=0,$$*

  - *$a_2$ is the only point satisfying
    $$\varphi'_-(a_2)=0 \quad\text{and}\quad \varphi'_+(a_2)>0.$$*
:::

::: corollary
**Corollary 1**. *For a data set $S=\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\},$ with $n=2p+1,$
$\varphi$ has an **absolute mininum (am)** $a_0$ satisfying:*

- *$a_0\in S,$*

- *$a_0$ is the only point satisfying
  $$\varphi'_-(a_0)<0 \quad\text{and}\quad \varphi'_+(a_0)>0.$$*
:::

We are now going to introduce algorithmically convenient formulas for
the left hand and right hand derivative of the function $\varphi.$ To
state these results we need some notations. For $v\in {\mathbb R},$ set
$$\begin{align*}
      L_v= &\{i:\  X_i<v\},\quad R_v=\{i:\  X_i>v\},\\
      l_v= &\#(L_v)\quad \text{and}\quad r_v= \#(R_v).
\end{align*}$$ We have the following lemma.

::: lemma
**Lemma 2**. *For $v\in {\mathbb R},$ we have:
$$\varphi'_-(v)=-n+2l_v \quad\text{and}\quad \varphi'_+(v)=n-2r_v .$$*
:::

Given $u,v\in {\mathbb R},$ the next result gives the relationships
between $l_u$ and $l_v$ and between $r_u$ and $r_v$. These relationships
will help in our algorithms, to speed up the computation of
$\varphi'_-(v)$ when $\varphi'_-(u)$ is known. To state this result, we
introduce the following notations. For $u,v \in {\mathbb R},$ $u<v$ we
set $$\begin{align*}
              E_u= &\{i:\ X_i=v\},\quad e_u=\#(E_u),\\
             S_{u,v}=&\{i:\ u< X_i<v\},\quad s_{u,v} =\#(S_{u,v}).
\end{align*}$$ If $l_v,\ r_v,\ e_v, \ e_u,$ and $s_{u,v}$ are known, the
lemma below shows that we can deduce $l_u$ and $r_u.$

::: lemma
**Lemma 3**. *For $u<v$ we have: $$\begin{align*}
       (i)\  \, l_u=& l_v-e_u-s_{u,v},\\
       (ii)\   r_u=& r_v+e_v+s_{u,v}.
\end{align*}$$*
:::

The proofs of Lemma 2 and Lemma 3 are in the supplementary material.

# Basic principles of our methods  {#sec:3}

In this section, we introduce notations and properties common to both
dichotomy and gradient descent. Let
$f:{\mathbb R}\rightarrow {\mathbb R}$ be a convex and differentiable
function. It is well known that a minimizer of $f$ is a solution of the
equation $f'(x)=0.$ When it is not possible to solve $f'(x)=0$
analytically, usually dichotomy or gradient descent is used to build an
approximate solution. In this paper, we want to minimize the convex
function $\varphi$, however $\varphi$ is not differentiable.
Nonetheless, $\varphi_{-}'(t)$ exists for all $t.$ In this section we
show how we can use $\varphi_{-}'(t)$ to compute **lm**.

Lemma 4 belows gives a useful characterization of **lm**; its proof is
the supplementary material.

::: lemma
**Lemma 4**. *$$\mathbf{lm}=\max\{ v:\quad \varphi_{-}'(v)<0
          \}.$$*
:::

Lemma 4 is very interesting, it can be used to test whether an interval
contains **lm**. Le $a<b$, we have:

- if $\varphi_{-}'(a)<0$ and $\varphi_{-}'(b)\ge 0$ then
  $\mathbf{lm}\in [a,\ b[;$

- if $\varphi_{-}'(a)\ge 0$ then $\mathbf{lm}\notin [a,\ b];$

- if $\varphi_{-}'(b)< 0$ then $\mathbf{lm}\notin [a,\ b[.$

The function $\varphi_{-}'(v)$ plays important roles in the rest of the
paper. To save typing and space we set $$\rho(v)=\varphi_{-}'(v).$$ We
now introduce some notations used in the sequel. Let $U$ be a vector in
${\mathbb R}^p$ that is $U=(u_1,\ldots,u_p)$ for
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_q)\in \{1,2,\ldots,p\}^q \ (q\leq p)$ we set
$$U(I)=(u_{i_1},u_{i_2},\ldots,u_{i_q}).$$ Let $e\in{\mathbb R},$
$K=\{i\ : \ u_i<e\}=\{j_1,\ldots,J_{q_1}\}$ with
$j_1<j_2<\ldots<j_{q_1}.$ We define the vector $(U<e)$ by
$$(U<e)=U(J)\quad \text{where}\quad J=(j_1,\ldots,J_{q_1}).$$ Likewise
the vector $(U\ge e)$ is defined by $$(U\ge e)=U(J')$$ where
$$J'=(j_1',\ldots,J_{q_2}'),\quad \{j_1',\ldots,J_{q_2}'\}=\{i\ : \ u_i\ge e\}\quad \text{and}\quad j_1'<j_2'<\ldots<j_{q_2}'.$$
Let $V=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\in {\mathbb R}^m,$ in what follows we write
$U\subseteq V$ if every component of $U$ is a component of $V,$ said
otherwise $u_i\in \{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}.$ For a vector $V=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)$
we define $\lvert V\rvert$ as
$$\lvert V\rvert=\mathrm{card}(\{v_i,\ 1\leq i\leq m \}).$$

The common ideas used in the methods considered in this article consists
in building a sequence
$\left(a_i,b_i,c_i,M_i \right)_{i\in {\mathbb N}^*}$ such that:

- $a_i\leq c_i\leq b_i,$$\mathbf{lm}\in [a_i,\ b_i],$$[a_{i+1},\ b_{i+1}] \subseteq [a_i,\ b_i] ;$

- $M_i\subseteq X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n),$$M_{i+1}\subseteq M_i;$

- $\exists m_0\in {\mathbb N},\quad a_{m_0}=\mathbf{lm}=b_{m_0}.$

Below in Step-1, Step-2, Step-3 we present the construction of the
sequence $\left(a_i,b_i,c_i,M_i \right).$

- *construction of $\left(a_1,b_1,c_1,M_1 \right)$*

  - $a_1=\min(S);$

  - $b_1=\max(S);$

  - $M_1=(X_1,\ldots,X_n);$

  - `if` $(a_1=b_1)$

    - $c_1= a_1;$

  - `if` $(a_1<b_1)$

    - `choose` $c_1\in ]a_1,\ b_1[;$

- *construction of $\left(a_2,b_2,c_2,M_2 \right)$* :

  - $L=(M_1<c_1);$

  - $R=(M_1>=c_1);$

  - `if` $(\rho(c_1)<0)$

    - `if` $(L=\emptyset)$

      - $a_2=\min(R);$

      - $b_2=b_1;$

    - `if` $(L\neq\emptyset)$

      - $a_2=c_1;$

      - $b_2=b_1;$

    - $M_2=R;$

  - `if` $(\rho(c_1)\ge 0)$

    - `if` $(R=\emptyset)$

      - $b_2=\max(L);$

      - $a_2=a_1;$

    - `if` $(R\neq\emptyset)$

      - $b_2=c_1;$

      - $a_2= a_1;$

    - $M_2=L;$

  - `if` $(a_2=b_2)$

    - $c_2= a_2;$

  - `if` $(a_2<b_2)$

    - `choose` $c_2\in ]a_2,\ b_2[;$

- *induction step, construction of
  $\left(a_{k+1},b_{k+1},c_{k+1},M_{k+1} \right)$* :

  - $L=(M_k<c_k);$

  - $R=(M_k>=c_k);$

  - `if` $(\rho(c_k)<0)$

    - `if` $(L=\emptyset)$

      - $a_{k+1}=\min(R);$

      - $b_{k+1}=b_k;$

    - `if` $(L\neq\emptyset)$

      - $a_{k+1}=c_k;$

      - $b_{k+1}=b_k;$

    - $M_{k+1}=R;$

  - `if` $(\rho(c_k)\ge 0)$

    - `if` $(R=\emptyset)$

      - $b_{k+1}=\max(L);$

      - $a_{k+1}=a_k;$

    - `if` $(R\neq\emptyset)$

      - $b_{k+1}=c_k;$

      - $a_{k+1}= a_k;$

    - $M_{k+1}=L;$

  - `if` $(a_{k+1}=b_{k+1})$

    - $c_{k+1}= a_{k+1};$

  - `if` $(a_{k+1}<b_{k+1})$

    - `choose` $c_{k+1}\in ]a_{k+1},\ b_{k+1}[;$

::: definition
**Definition 1**. *A sequence
$\left(\Omega_k=\left(a_k,b_k,c_k,M_k \right),\quad k\in {\mathbb N}^*\right)$
built recursively by Step-1---Step-3 presented above is called a generic
sequence.*
:::

In Proposition 1--4 below are listed some interesting properties of the
sequence $\left(a_i,b_i,c_i,M_i \right)_{i\in {\mathbb N}^*}.$ The
proofs of these results are in the supplementary material.

::: proposition
**Proposition 1**. *If
$\lvert M_k\rvert\geq 2,\  \lvert M_{k+1}\rvert =\lvert M_k\rvert$ and
$\lvert M_{k+2}\rvert=\lvert M_k\rvert$ then
$$\lvert M_{k+3}\rvert < \lvert M_k\rvert.$$*
:::

::: proposition
**Proposition 2**. *If $\lvert M_k\rvert\geq 2,$ $\exists j>k$ such
that: $$\lvert M_{j}\rvert < \lvert M_k\rvert.$$*
:::

::: proposition
**Proposition 3**. *There exists $p_0\in{\mathbb N}$ such that:
$$\lvert M_{p_0}\rvert =1.$$*
:::

::: proposition
**Proposition 4**. *There exists $m_0\in{\mathbb N}$ such that:
$$a_{m_0}=\mathbf{lm}= b_{m_0}.$$*
:::

# Dichotomy {#sec:3}

This approach is based on Lemma 4. It is very similar to the classical
dichotomy used to find the zero of a function. The main idea here is to
use $\varphi_{-}'(v)$ to build a sequence converging to $\mathbf{lm}.$
The dichotomic sequence is introduce in Definition 2 below.

::: definition
**Definition 2**. *A sequence
$\left(\mathscr{A}_k=\left(a_k,b_k,c_k,M_k \right),\quad k\in {\mathbb N}^*\right)$
is called a dichotomic sequence if it is built recursively by Step-a1
and Step-a2 presented in the supplementary material.*
:::

It is clear that a dichotomic sequence is a generic sequence, thus we
have: $\lim a_k=\mathbf{lm}=\lim b_k.$ The dichotomic algorithm is
implemented in the (matlab) mex-file median_rouen_dic given in the
supplementary material. Table 1 contains computational times of
median_rouen_dic and those of the build-in matlab function median when
the sample is "small\". This table shows clearly that, the performance
of median_rouen_dic is superior to that of matlab median when the sample
size is between 10 and 150.

From Table 2 we see that, the runtime of the program median_rouen_dic
increases with the sample size $n.$ This is because the number of
comparisons increase with $n.$ The runtime of matlab median also
increases with the sample size. It also appears from this table that the
performance of median_rouen_dic is slightly superior to that of matlab
median for "medium\" sample sizes.

# Gradient descent {#sec:4}

## Plain descent method  {#sec:4.1}

This approach borrows a lot from the classical gradient descent
algorithm. Before its introduction, let us recall the basic tools of the
gradient descent. Let $f:{\mathbb R}\longrightarrow {\mathbb R}$ be a
convex differentiable function. Assume that we want to find a minimizer
of $f.$ The gradient descent method consists in building a sequence
$(x_n)_{n\in{\mathbb N}}$ converging to a minimizer of $f.$ The sequence
is constructed as follows:

- Select an arbitrary starting point $x_0;$

- Choose a learning rate $\delta >0;$

- The sequence is defined recursively as
  $$x_{n+1}=x_n -\delta f'(x_n).$$

The theory shows that, under certain regularity conditions of $f,$ there
exists $\delta_0>0$ such that
$$0<\delta<\delta_0 \implies x_n\quad\text{converges to}\quad w_0$$
where $w_0$ is a minimizer of $f.$ Some comments regarding the
construction of the sequence are in order here. If $f'(x_n)>0,$ then f
is increasing in a neighborhood of $x_n.$ Thus, the minimizer of $f$ is
less than $x_n,$ this is why $x_{n+1}$ is chosen such that
$$x_{n+1}=x_n -\delta f'(x_n)<x_n.$$ If $f'(x_n)<0,$ then
$$x_n<  x_{n+1}=x_n -\delta f'(x_n).$$ This means that $x_{n+1}$ is
chosen to the left of $x_n$ when the gradient is positive and to the
right when the gradient is negative: we move against the gradient. We
now illustrate the working of the gradient descent on a simple example.
Let $a$ be a fixed real and $f(x)={\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^2}.$ It is clear
that $f$ has a unique minimum at $w_0=a.$ We have:$f'(x)=x-a,$ therefore
the sequence $(x_n)_{n\in {\mathbb N}}$ is defined recursively by
$$\begin{align*}
          x_{n+1} & =x_n-\delta (x_n-a) \\
                  & =(1-\delta) x_n+ \delta a.
\end{align*}$$ Because $a=(1-\delta) a+\delta a,$ we see that
$$x_{n+1}-a   =(1-\delta) (x_n-a)$$ it follows that
$$x_n-a=(1-\delta)^n (x_0-a)\iff x_n=a+ (1-\delta)^n (x_0-a).$$
Therefore we have: $$\lim x_n=a \iff -1<1-\delta <1\iff 0<\delta<2.$$

We introduce the following definition.

::: definition
**Definition 3**. *A sequence
$\left(\mathscr{B}_k=\left(a_k,b_k,c_k,M_k \right),\quad k\in {\mathbb N}^*\right)$
is called a gradient descent sequence if it is built recursively by
Step-b1 and Step-b2 given in the supplementary material.*
:::

Proposition 5 below will allow us to state some properties of a gradient
descent sequence. Let $a<b,$ and set
$m=\mathrm{card}(\{i:\ a\leq X_i\leq b\})$. We have the following useful
result.

::: proposition
**Proposition 5**. *If $\varphi_{-}'(a)<0$ and
$\left(\varphi_{-}'(b)>0\right.$ or $\left( \varphi_{-}'(b)=0 \right.$
and $\left.\left.\varphi_{+}'(b)>0\right)\right)$ then
$$-1<\frac{\varphi_{-}'(a)}{2m}<0.$$*
:::

The proof of Proposition 5 is in the supplementary material.

We now present the intuition behind the gradient descent sequence. Let
$a<b,$ we assume that
$\varphi_{-}'(a)<0 \quad\text{and}\quad \varphi_{+}'(b)>0$, so that
$\mathbf{lm}, \mathbf{gm}\in [a,\ b].$ We need the following notations
$$M=(a\leq M_1\leq b)\quad\text{where}\quad M_1=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$$ thus
$X_i$ is a component of the vector M if $a\leq X_i\leq b$. To save space
we set $$M=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$$ therefore we assume that
$\mathtt{length}(M)=m=\mathrm{card}\{i:\ a\leq X_i\leq b\}.$ In what
follows it is important to remember that $\mathbf{lm}$ and $\mathbf{gm}$
are components of the vector $M.$ Given $a,b,M,m$ defined above, the
gradient descent algorithm chooses $c\in(a,\ b)$ by the formula
$$c= a -\frac{\varphi_{-}'(a)}{2m} (b-a).$$ We want to explain how this
formula is obtained. We also assume that $n=2p$ and
$\mathbf{lm}<\mathbf{gm},$ because the intuition is easier to "see" in
this situation. We set $$\begin{align*}
         r_M(\mathbf{lm})= & \sum_{j=1}^m\,\rlap{{\rm \Large 1}}\kern.30em \mbox{\rm \Large l}_{[Z_i \leq \mathbf{lm} ]},\\
         t_0=a, & \quad t_j=a+ \frac{j}{m}(b-a),\quad j=1,\ldots,m.
\end{align*}$$ The gradient descent algorithm chooses $t_{j_0}$ in
$(a,\ b)$ if $$r_M(\mathbf{lm})=j_0.$$ This means that the chosen point
is "close" to $b$ when $r_M(\mathbf{lm})$ is large and "close" to $a$
when $r_M(\mathbf{lm})$ is small. Indeed, let
$c\in (\mathbf{lm},\  \mathbf{gm}),$ we have $$\begin{align*}
               \varphi_{-}'(c)=0 &=\varphi_{-}'(a)+2\sum_{i=1}^n \,\rlap{{\rm \Large 1}}\kern.30em \mbox{\rm \Large l}_{[X_i <c]} \,\rlap{{\rm \Large 1}}\kern.30em \mbox{\rm \Large l}_{[a\leq X_i \leq b]}\\
                                 &=\varphi_{-}'(a)+2\sum_{j=1}^m \,\rlap{{\rm \Large 1}}\kern.30em \mbox{\rm \Large l}_{[Z_i <c]}\\ 
                                 &=\varphi_{-}'(a)+2 r_M(\mathbf{lm}).
\end{align*}$$ It follows that
$$r_M(\mathbf{lm})=-\frac{\varphi_{-}'(a)}{2}$$ hence $$\begin{align*}
             c= & a -\frac{\varphi_{-}'(a)}{2m} (b-a)\\
              = & a+\frac{r_M(\mathbf{lm})}{m}(b-a)\\
              = & t_{r_M(\mathbf{lm})}.
\end{align*}$$ Why do we talk about gradient descent (regarding this
approach)? Because when $a_k<b_k,$ $a_{k+1},b_{k+1}$ and $M_{k+1}$ are
derived from $\left(a_k,b_k,c_k,M_k \right)$ using $\varphi_{-}'(c_k).$
Moreover by setting $$\begin{align*}
             L_k=& (M_k<c_k),\\
             R_k= &(M_k\geq c_k),\\
             m_k=&\mathtt{length}(M_k),\\
             \lambda_k=&(b_k-a_k)/2m_k,
\end{align*}$$ if $(\varphi_{-}'(c_k)<0)$ and $(L_k\neq \emptyset)$ we
have: $$\begin{align*}
             a_{k+1}=& c_k\\
                    = & a_k-\lambda_k \varphi_{-}'(a_k).
\end{align*}$$ And, this formula resembles the classical gradient
descent formula.

We describe below two situations in which a gradient descent sequence
converges to **lm**.

If $n=2p+1$

By Corollary 1 we know that:
$$\mathbf{lm}=\mathbf{am},\quad \varphi_{-}'(\mathbf{lm})<0,\quad \varphi_{+}'(\mathbf{lm})>0.$$
Since by construction $a_k\leq \mathbf{lm}\leq b_k,$ we deduce that
$$\varphi_{-}'(a_k)<0 \quad\text{and}\quad \varphi_{+}'(b_k)>0,\quad \forall k\in {\mathbb N}^*,$$
because $x\mapsto \varphi_{-}'(x)$ and $x\mapsto \varphi_{+}'(x)$ are
nondecreasing functions. If $a_k<b_k,$ then by the gradient descent
algorithm we have: $$\begin{align*}
        c_k=& a_k-r\rho(a_k)\\
           =& a_k-r\varphi_{-}'(a_k)\quad (\text{definition of}\ \rho )\\
           =& a_k -\frac{\varphi_{-}'(a_k)}{2m} (b_k-a_k).\quad  (m=\mathtt{length}( M_k))
\end{align*}$$ Because of Proposition 5 we have
$0< -\frac{\varphi_{-}'(a_k)}{2m}<1,$ thus we deduce that
$c_k \in (a_k,\ b_k).$ This fact shows that the gradient descent
sequence is a generic sequence. Therefore the sequences
$\left(a_k\right)_{k\in {\mathbb N}^*}$ and
$\left(b_k\right)_{k\in {\mathbb N}^*}$ converge to **lm.**

If $n=2p$ and $\mathbf{lm}=\mathbf{gm}$

In this case we know that $\mathbf{lm}=\mathbf{am},$ so by Theorem 1 we
have: $$\varphi_{-}'(\mathbf{lm})<0,\quad \varphi_{+}'(\mathbf{lm})>0.$$
Therefore, as in the case $n=2p+1$ we have
$$\lim a_k=\mathbf{lm}=\lim b_k.$$

The case $n=2p$ and $\mathbf{lm}<\mathbf{gm}$ is more difficult to
analyze. When this condition is true, we know that (see the proof of
Theorem 1) $$\begin{align*}
         \varphi_{-}'(\mathbf{lm})< & 0,\quad \varphi_{+}'(\mathbf{lm})=0,\\
         \varphi'(t)= &0,\quad \forall t\in (\mathbf{lm},\ \mathbf{gm}),\\
         \varphi_{-}'(\mathbf{gm})= & 0,\quad \varphi_{+}'(\mathbf{gm})>0.
\end{align*}$$ Using inequalities and equalities above, we can prove
that $$\begin{align*}
        \varphi_{-}'(t)< & 0,\quad \text{for}\quad t\in (-\infty,\ \mathbf{lm}),\quad  
        \varphi_{-}'(t)= 0,\quad \text{for}\quad t\in (\mathbf{lm},\ \mathbf{gm}],\quad\\
       \varphi_{-}'(t)> & 0,\quad \text{for}\quad t\in (\mathbf{gm},\ +\infty).
\end{align*}$$

The set $W_0$ defined by $$W_0=(\mathbf{lm},\ \mathbf{gm}]$$ and
Definition 4 introduced below play important roles in the rest of this
subsection.

::: definition
**Definition 4**. *A sequence
$\left(\mathscr{C}_k=\left(a_k,b_k,c_k,M_k \right),\quad k\in {\mathbb N}^*\right)$
is called a mix sequence if it is built recursively by Step-c1 and
Step-c2 presented in the supplementary material.*
:::

Lemma 5--7 below will help us to prove some properties of the gradient
descent sequence. Their proofs are in the supplementary material.

::: lemma
**Lemma 5**. *Let
$\left(\mathscr{C}_k=\left(a_k,b_k,c_k,M_k \right),\quad k\in {\mathbb N}^*\right)$
be a mix sequence. If $n=2p$ and $\mathbf{lm}<\mathbf{gm},$ we have:
$$c_1,\ldots,c_q\notin W_0\implies a_1\leq\cdots \leq a_{q+1}\leq \mathbf{lm}<\mathbf{gm}\leq b_{q+1}\leq \cdots \leq b_1.$$*
:::

::: lemma
**Lemma 6**. *Let
$\left(\mathscr{C}_k=\left(a_k,b_k,c_k,M_k \right),\quad k\in {\mathbb N}^*\right)$
be a mix sequence. If $n=2p$ and $\mathbf{lm}<\mathbf{gm},$ we have:
$$a_k<b_k\implies c_k\in (a_k,\ b_k).$$*
:::

::: lemma
**Lemma 7**. *Let
$\left(\mathscr{C}_k=\left(a_k,b_k,c_k,M_k \right),\quad k\in {\mathbb N}^*\right)$
be a mix sequence. If $n=2p$ and $\mathbf{lm}<\mathbf{gm},$ there exists
$k_0\in {\mathbb N}^*$ such that:
$$c_{k_0}\in (\mathbf{lm},\ \mathbf{gm}].$$*
:::

The property of the mix sequence stated in Lemma 7 is also valid for the
gradient descent sequence. This Property is given in Proposition 6
below. The proof of Proposition 6 is in the supplementary material.

::: proposition
**Proposition 6**. *Let
$\left(\mathscr{B}_k=\left(a_k,b_k,c_k,M_k \right),\quad k\in {\mathbb N}^*\right)$
be a gradient descent sequence. If $n=2p$ and $\mathbf{lm}<\mathbf{gm},$
there exists $q_0\in {\mathbb N}^*$ such that:
$$c_{q_0}\in (\mathbf{lm},\ \mathbf{gm}].$$*
:::

Proposition 6 is very important for the gradient descent approach when
$n=2p$ and $\mathbf{lm}<\mathbf{gm}.$ Let
$\left(\mathscr{B}_k=\left(a_k,b_k,c_k,M_k \right),\quad k\in {\mathbb N}^*\right)$
be a gradient descent sequence and set
$$q_0=\min\{ k,\quad c_k\in (\mathbf{lm},\ \mathbf{gm}]\}.$$ In the
implementation of the gradient descent we will only build
$$\left(a_1,b_1,c_1,M_1 \right),\dots,\left(a_{q_0},b_{q_0},c_{q_0},M_{q_0} \right).$$
Because we know how to find $\mathbf{lm}$ and $\mathbf{gm}$ in $M_{q_0}$
when $c_{q_0}$ is found.

The gradient descent algorithm is implemented in the program
median_rouen_gra given in the supplementary material. In Tables 4-6 are
presented the results of our experimentations designed to compare matlab
median and median_rouen_gra. The performance of median_rouen_gra
(relatively to that of matlab median) is grossly similar to that of
median_rouen_dic. Table 4 shows that the runtime of median_rouen_gra is
better than that of matlab median when the sample size is "small\";
Table 5 shows superiority of median_rouen_gra to matlab median for
"medium\" sample sizes; in Table 6 matlab median is superior to
median_rouen_gra when the sample size is 1 million while
median_rouen_gra performs better than matlab median when the sample size
is between 2 million and 8 million.

## Truncated gradient descent  {#sec:4.2}

This approach is a modification of the gradient descent method. In this
subsection, we only mention how the gradient descent is modified. Let
$\left(\mathscr{G}_k=\left(a_k,b_k,c_k,M_k \right),\quad k\in {\mathbb N}^*\right)$
be the gradient descent sequence, let us recall how $c_k$ is "chosen\"
in $(a_k,\ b_k)$ when
$\varphi_{-}'(a_k)<0\quad\text{and}\quad \varphi_{+}'(b_k)>0$: $c_k$ is
given by
$$c_k=a_k+h_k (b_k-a_k)\quad\text{where}\quad h_k=-\left(\frac{\varphi_{-}'(a_k)}{2m_k}\right),\quad
         m_k=\mathtt{length}(M_k).$$ Let us also recall the following
vectors useful in the sequel:
$$R=R_k=\left(M_k\geq c_k\right),\quad  L=L_k=\left(M_k< c_k\right).$$
It follows from the formula of $c_k$ that, if $h_k$ is close to 1, then
$c_k$ is close $b_k.$ When $c_k$ is close to $b_k$ the likelihood of
getting $R=R_k=\emptyset$ is high. And, when $R=\emptyset$ we know that
$$b_{k+1}=\max(L)$$ thus the computation of $b_{k+1}$ is time consuming.
If $h_k$ is close to 0, the risk of getting $L=L_k=\emptyset$ is also
high. When $L=\emptyset$ the computation of $a_{k+1}$ is costly. To
avoid these situations from happening, we truncate $h_k$ in the
following manner. Let $\alpha\in(0,\ \frac{1}{2})$ we set
$$\bar{h}_k = \begin{cases} \alpha, & \text{if}\quad h_k < \alpha, \\ 
                                    h_k, & \text{if}\quad\alpha \leq h_k\leq 1-\alpha, \\
                                     1-\alpha, &\text{if}\quad h_k > 1-\alpha, 
                     \end{cases}$$ and, $c_k$ in the truncated gradient
descent is defined by $$c_k=a_k+\bar{h}_k (b_k-a_k).$$

The truncated gradient descent algorithm is implemented in the matlab
(mex) program median_rouen_tru presented in the supplementary material.
In Tables 7--9 are summarized our computations regarding the truncated
gradient descent method. These tables reveal that the runtime of
median_rouen_tru is better than that of the built-in matlab median for
all samples sizes.

The truncation parameter $\alpha$ used in the truncated method is
supposed to satisfy $0<\alpha<\frac{1}{2}.$ If we "choose\"
$\alpha=\frac{1}{2}$ we get the dichotomic approach, if $\alpha=0$ we
get the "plain gradient\" algorithm. This observation shows that each
one of our approaches can be considered a special case of the truncated
gradient method. When the samples sizes are "small" the best results are
obtained by plain gradient and the truncated gradient. The best results
are obtained by the plain gradient approach and dichotomy when the
samples sizes are "medium", and the "truncated gradient\" has the best
results when $n$ is "large.\" Those facts suggest that we should
"choose" $\alpha$ as a function of the sample size. We hope to consider
the problem of selecting $\alpha=\alpha_n$ in a future paper.

Assume that the medians compute by the matlab build-in function are
stored in the vector $V_{mat}=(u_1,\ldots,u_r),$ where $r$ is the number
of replications. Similarly suppose that the medians computed by
median_rouen_dic (respectively median_rouen_grad, median_rouen_tru) are
stored in the vector $V_{rou}=(v_1,\ldots,v_r).$ In the simulations we
have also computed the quantities: $$Error=\sum_{i=1}^{r} (u_i-v_i)^2.$$
These quantities are not reported because they are all equal to zero.
This shows that the methods introduced in this paper give the same
results as the matlab build-in function.
